## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sakka Saṁyutta* (SN 11; also titled *Sakkasaṁyutta*) is the eleventh collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Sagāthāvagga* [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Sujato 2012]. The text comprises twenty-five discourses arranged across three chapters (*vagga*), featuring both substantive prose narratives and extended verse dialogues [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Bingenheimer]. The collection centers on Sakka, the ruler of the thirty-three gods (*Tāvatiṁsa*), who attained celestial kingship by virtue of past meritorious deeds [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994]. Rather than retaining the bellicose traits of his Vedic counterpart Indra, Sakka is recast as a devoted follower of the Buddha who champions virtues of non-violence, patience, and forgiveness [Amerbauer 2000; Bingenheimer]. A primary narrative theme is the conflict between the gods and the *asuras* led by Vepacitti (whom Sakka refers to as an "older god"), in which Sakka demonstrates moral restraint and forbearance even when provoked or insulted [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994; Sujato 2011].

Scholars note that grouping verses of homage around a specific deity in collections like the *Sakka Saṁyutta* mirrors pre-Buddhist organizing principles found in Vedic literature [Sujato 2012]. The collection has extensive parallels across early Buddhist literature, with twenty-six discourses mapped to corresponding texts in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ / T 99, split between fascicles 40 and 46) and the 'other' *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ² / T 100 / BZA), alongside parallels in the *Ekottarikāgama* [SuttaCentral; Bingenheimer]. Individual discourses show wide circulation: the protective *Dhajagga Sutta* (SN 11.3) parallels versions in the Tibetan *Mahāsūtras* (D 292, *Dhvajāgra-nāma-mahāsūtra*), while Prajñāvarman's commentary on the *Udānavarga* (*Udānavargavivaraṇa*, D 4100) preserves a parallel to the *Vepacittisutta* (SN 11.4) [SuttaCentral; Bingenheimer; Skilling]. Automatic alignment by DharmaNexus confirms broad textual reuse with Chinese Āgamas (T 1, T 23, T 24, T 99, T 100), the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* and *Mahāvastu*, the Tibetan *Vinayavastu*, and extensive Pali-internal overlap with the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and various *Aṅguttaranikāya* nipātas [DharmaNexus].
